details:
GLORPULSE is a web app for a simulated Mars transit with several astronaut profiles. Each astronaut logs a daily check-in: heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, sleep, mood and symptoms, plus blood glucose for crew members who track it. The app compares each new reading with that astronaut's own seven-day baseline, built from the median and spread of their first week. It then shows three things:

  • whether the latest reading is above, within or below their own baseline,
  • how many days in a row a change has lasted,
  • an Info, Watch or Action alert, using rules shown on screen.

Charts show readings over time with the baseline band. A reference range is drawn only when a verified source exists. Each astronaut's data is kept separate, and a reset button restores the demo data.

What are the benefits?

  • Astronauts see what changed for them personally, not only a colour against a general range.
  • Guidance is limited to what a verified source supports. Otherwise the app says "No sourced guidance available".
  • Status never relies on colour alone, and the app works in the browser with no server or sign-in.

What is the intended impact? On a Mars mission, a one-way message takes roughly 4 to 24 minutes, and astronauts may not be able to get quick help. GLORPULSE helps a non-expert notice early changes, understand them in plain language, and decide when to ask a flight surgeon. It is decision support, not diagnosis.

What tools and technology did you use? React, Vite and TypeScript (strict mode), Recharts for charts, plain CSS, and browser localStorage for entered data. Vitest checks the health-logic rules. There is no backend or database. We planned and built it with Kiro as our AI development assistant, and no special hardware was used.

How is it creative?

  • The personal baseline and the length of a deviation, instead of a single coloured dot.
  • Three kinds of comparison are kept strictly apart: the astronaut's own baseline, a published reference range, and mission limits.
  • A briefing prepared for the moment the link returns, which fits the real communication delay.
  • Honest limits: the app shows "building baseline" and "not assessed" instead of guessing.

What did your team consider?

  • Safety: no invented medical thresholds, no diagnosis, a disclaimer everywhere, and a Contact Flight Surgeon level deliberately left without an automatic trigger until a sourced or clearly labelled rule exists.
  • Evidence: every medical statement needs a verified NASA or other source.
  • Privacy: all data is simulated and nothing is sent over a network.
  • Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 AA is our goal, not a claim. Controls work by keyboard and status uses text and icons.
  • Scope: two beginners and 48 hours, so we cut machine learning, wearables, 3D, live NASA feeds and a backend.
  • Competition: other teams build large systems, so we focused on clear, sourced explanations.
